newsitem.title: USA: Connie Lee may need more capital to compete - report.
newsitem.headline: Connie Lee may need more capital to compete - report.

text.p: Connie Lee Insurance Co may need to increase its capital as much as 64 percent to compete successfully in its new expanded market, according to a report on the company's recent privatization.
Connie Lee currently carries a AAA rating from Standard & Poor's Corp, but in contrast to its main competitors in the muni market, is not rated by Moody's Investors Service Inc.
The report, written by A.G. Edwards & Sons analyst Julie Peckham, said Connie Lee may need obtain a Moody's rating and may also be required to raise more capital to keep its AAA grade from S&P.

"We feel that with an expanded business focus, Connie Lee may find it necessary to apply for additional ratings on its claims-paying ability in order to compete with the other insurers," the report says. Peckham estimated Moody's would require about $200 million in capital for a Aaa rating, or a 64 percent increase in Connie Lee's existing level.
"A capital increase of this magnitude could not be generated quickly from operations and thus is not likely in the near future without a capital infusion from outside sources," the report says.
Connie Lee officials were not immediately available for comment on the report.

U.S. Congress privatized Connie Lee in 1996, and the process was completely earlier this year when the U.S. Department of Education sold off its remaining stake in the company. The move permitted Connie Lee to begin expanding beyond its original Congressional mandate of insuring bonds issued by educational institutions.

Despite the need for more capital, Peckham said she sees Connie Lee's privatization as a positive, and believes the 10 to 15 basis point spread the market currently demands for Connie Lee bonds will tighten over time if the Moody's rating is obtained and capital levels increase.

"In the long run, increased demand and an additional rating should tighten the spread between bonds insured by Connie Lee and bonds backed by the major insurers," the report says. "Because of this potential, we believe that Connie Lee bonds represent upside potential and creates value for the buy-and-hold investor."
Oliver Sockwell, Connie Lee's president and chief executive officer, resigned last week, saying he wanted to pursue other interests now that the company's privatization was complete.
